beats.narration_text: Hey, this is Param Madan, and this explainer video is on units in the physics engine. Here's the story. An automatic check compared the units on every formula card, and found that one letter, T, meant a force on one card, and a time on two others. Force is not time. So that couldn't be a false alarm.

props.command: How does the physics engine check units, and what did that check find?
output: Every unit label must be a real dimension
Card units must match the variable dictionary
It caught T meaning both a force and a time

beats.narration_text: In the next few minutes, you'll see three things. First, why units matter in a physics answer. Second, what the engine's unit check does, and what it doesn't. And third, an honest swap: the tool the plan called for, and the one the team used instead. No physics or coding background needed.

The answer up front. Every formula card labels its answers with units. The engine now checks those labels automatically. Each one has to be a real physical unit, and it has to agree with the engine's dictionary of variables. What it doesn't do yet is carry units through the algebra itself. And the team says so plainly.

Why bother? Because a number without the right unit is a wrong answer. Speed in meters per second. Distance in meters. Tension in newtons. A period in seconds. Put centimeters into a formula that expects meters, and the answer is off by a factor of a hundred. One wave card's own warning is exactly that slip.

So the engine checks two things. First, every unit label must turn into a real dimension, like length divided by time. That catches typos and nonsense units. Second, each card's unit for a variable must match the dictionary's unit for that same variable. A card that says speed is measured in meters gets caught. Both checks are part of the engine's automated tests.

And it found a real defect. T was tension, a force in newtons, on the pulley card. And T was a period, a time in seconds, on the orbit and magnetic field cards. Someone had spotted that by hand before. Now a machine can detect it. Force versus time can't be a false alarm.

Today the dictionary says it out loud. T means tension, or period: read which from the problem. Same for R: a radius in meters, or a resistance in ohms. And in the team's words, this turns renaming the symbols someday from a judgment call into a check with an objective trigger.

beats.new_visual_element: pint was the plan; SymPy units ran
beats.narration_text: Now the honest part. The project plan called for a units library called pint. It couldn't be installed where the engine was built. So instead of writing code against a library that had never run even once, the team used SymPy's own units module, which did run. And they wrote down the limit. Units are checked on the labels, not carried through the solve. That's still open.

So here's the takeaway. A tool that says what it didn't do is worth more than one that claims it did everything. When an A.I. model gives you a physics answer, check its units first. If the units don't make sense, the number doesn't either.
Your turn. Paste this into Claude with any formula, or any answer. It asks Claude to check the units, step by step.

props.command: Here is a formula or an answer: [paste it]. Check its units step by step: write the unit of every symbol, combine them through each operation, and confirm the final unit matches what is being asked. Flag any step where the units do not agree.
